opus_only: Macroeconomic uncertainty as of mid-2023 is high relative to its own history when measured with a quantitative index.
Rate hikes compress bank margins, which appear as mark-to-market losses now and lower earnings later, while deposits shrink.
The JLN index summarises uncertainty across a large set of economic releases into one monthly number.
The 2010s were a decade of consistently below-average macro uncertainty, in contrast to the 2020s.
Beyond statistics, the current policy and market backdrop supports the view that uncertainty stays high.
Catalyst 1 for persistent uncertainty: lagged effects of aggressive hikes plus a new employment-inflation trade-off for central banks.
Example: in 1980 the Volcker Fed cut then re-hiked, showing how trade-offs produce abrupt policy reversals.
Example: front-end yield volatility in March 2023, when banking concerns caused sharp downward revisions to policy expectations.
Large swings in front-end rate pricing are a market sign of high economic uncertainty.
If long-run inflation expectations de-anchor, disinflation would require more unemployment because expectations drive actual inflation.
Rate and inflation markets may be pricing a sharp slowdown, but equities are not, so asset classes disagree with each other.
The author takes no view on who is right; the argument is only that disagreement implies volatility.
The author judges SVB/Signature unlikely to spark a systemic crisis because crises usually stem from asset-quality deterioration, not deposit mix or duration mismatch.
Forecasters raised real GDP growth forecasts by 40bp after end-February 2023, showing little expectation of an imminent calamity.
With high uncertainty, both a stagflation redux and a 1990s-style productivity boom are plausible, so a single-asset bet is riskier than usual.
Diversification into bonds, commodities, trend and alternatives is recommended at all times, not only when uncertainty is high.
The author firm manages a fund inside the SG Trend Index used as evidence, a potential conflict of interest.
sonnet_only: Key question of the note: will elevated macro uncertainty persist or revert to the 2010s low-uncertainty regime, and what follows for traditional assets and alternatives.
Backdrop as of May 2023: inflation well above target, funds rate highest since pre-GFC, unemployment lowest in over 50 years, banks hit by compressed margins and shrinking deposits.
Implied decay: JLN of 1.0 forecast to 0.98 next month and about 0.8 in a year (0.98^12).

One way to reconcile bond/futures pricing with survey forecasts is an imminent sharp slowdown, which would hurt equities, yet equities show no evidence of pricing a slowdown (cross-asset disagreement).

Footnote 11 (author's opinion): the March 2023 bank failures are unlikely to trigger a widespread crisis because of the Fed/Treasury liquidity response, real GDP forecasts revised up by 40 bp since end-February (Consensus Economics), and because systemic crises usually come from asset quality, not duration mismatch.
Figure 5 uses monthly returns, so peak-to-trough drawdown windows are measured on month-end data.
